measures.title: Law Enforcement Communication with Federal Immigration Authorities
measures.ballot_label: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution requiring law enforcement to notify the department of homeland security when a person is charged with either a violent crime or any crime if the person has a prior felony conviction if law enforcement cannot determine that the person is lawfully present in the United States?
plain: Police, corrections officers, and district attorney staff would have to notify the U.S. Department of Homeland Security within 72 hours when they charge someone with a violent crime, or any crime if the person has a prior felony conviction.
The notice is required only when officers cannot confirm the person is lawfully in the United States.
The requirement would be written into the state constitution.
measures.yes: A yes vote requires law enforcement to notify federal immigration authorities in those cases.
measures.no: A no vote keeps current law, which has no such constitutional notification requirement.
measures.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates about $60,000 in one-time state costs in FY 2026-27 for database access and computer updates, with no ongoing state cost and some added local workload.

measures.title: Constitutional Right to Purchase and Sell Natural Gas
measures.ballot_label: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution creating new law granting the right for consumers to purchase natural gas for cooking or heating in homes or businesses and for distributors and utilities to sell natural gas to consumers?
plain: Creates a constitutional right for consumers to buy natural gas for cooking or heating in homes and businesses.
Creates a matching right for distributors and utilities to sell natural gas for those uses.
Local building codes that restrict natural gas would have to be changed to fit the new right.
measures.yes: A yes vote adds a right to buy and sell natural gas for cooking and heating to the state constitution.
measures.no: A no vote leaves the constitution unchanged, so state and local governments keep their current authority over natural gas use.
measures.fiscal: No direct state revenue or spending change is estimated; state agency workload may rise and local governments with gas-restricting building codes would face costs to conform them.

measures.title: Constitutional Right to Hunt and Fish
measures.ballot_label: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution creating a constitutional right to hunt, fish, and harvest fish and wildlife by traditional methods, including all species of fish and wildlife managed by the state except non-game species, endangered species, or any species that is illegal to hunt under federal law, ...
plain: Adds a right to hunt, fish, and harvest wildlife by traditional methods to the state constitution.
Does not cover non-game species, endangered species, or species that are illegal to hunt under federal law.
Makes hunting and fishing the preferred way to manage wildlife, while the state keeps its power to regulate for conservation and public safety.
measures.yes: A yes vote creates a constitutional right to hunt and fish in Colorado.
measures.no: A no vote leaves hunting and fishing governed by current statutes and regulations without a constitutional right.
measures.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff expects no change to near-term state revenue or spending.

measures.title: Mail Ballot Voter Identification
measures.ballot_label: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution requiring a voter to sign and include the last four digits of their social security number or their Colorado driver's license or identification card number on the outside of their mail ballot for any federal or state election, ...
plain: Mail voters would have to sign and write the last four digits of their Social Security number, or their Colorado driver's license or ID number, on the outside of the ballot envelope.
Voters could fix missing or wrong information, including with other forms of ID.
County clerks could not count a mail ballot until the problem is fixed.
measures.yes: A yes vote adds an ID-number requirement for mail ballots in federal and state elections.
measures.no: A no vote keeps the current signature-and-affirmation process for mail ballots.
measures.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates Department of State costs of $1.2 million in FY 2026-27, $260,000 in FY 2027-28, and $555,500 in FY 2028-29, plus county costs up to $2.5 million in 2026-27 (about 45% reimbursed by the state).

measures.title: Plain Language Ballot Titles
measures.ballot_label: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution concerning ballot question language, and, in connection therewith, requiring all state and local ballot questions to be written in plain language and at no more than an 8th grade reading level and prohibiting a state statute from requiring language that conflicts with these requirements in ballot questions for citizen-initiated measures?
plain: All state and local ballot questions would have to be written in plain language at no higher than an 8th-grade reading level.
State laws could not require wording in citizen-initiated ballot questions that conflicts with this rule.
The Title Board would set the standards for plain language and reading level.
measures.yes: A yes vote requires plain-language, 8th-grade-level ballot questions statewide.
measures.no: A no vote keeps current rules for how ballot questions are written.
measures.fiscal: No change in state revenue or spending; the Title Board may see minimal added workload.

measures.title: Requirements for Off-Cycle Congressional Redistricting
measures.ballot_label: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution concerning congressional redistricting, and, in connection therewith, reenacting the current process for congressional redistricting in the Colorado Constitution and prohibiting modifications to a final map unless at least three public meetings are held, ...
plain: Re-enacts Colorado's current independent commission process for drawing congressional districts.
Blocks changes to a final map unless at least three public meetings are held and the changes do not split communities of interest or purposely favor one party.
Any mid-decade map change would need approval from both the redistricting commission and the Colorado Supreme Court.
measures.yes: A yes vote requires commission and Supreme Court approval and public meetings before any off-cycle change to congressional maps.
measures.no: A no vote keeps the current process, which reviews maps only after each ten-year census.
measures.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates about $370,000 in state costs and 1.0 FTE only in a year when off-cycle redistricting occurs, and no cost otherwise.

measures.title: Graduated Income Tax
measures.ballot_label: Shall state taxes be increased $2.7 billion annually, in order to increase or improve levels of public services, including K-12 public school education, health care, and early child care and education services, by an amendment to the Colorado Constitution and a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes ...
plain: Replaces Colorado's flat 4.4% income tax with graduated rates that rise with income, and removes the constitution's single-rate rule in TABOR.
The 4.4% rate stays for income from selling a primary home.
New revenue goes to the Colorado Future's Account for K-12 schools, health care, and early child care; the state may keep and spend it without TABOR refunds.
measures.yes: A yes vote creates a graduated income tax and dedicates the added revenue to education, health care, and child care.
measures.no: A no vote keeps the flat 4.4% income tax.
measures.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates state revenue rises $958.4 million in FY 2026-27 (half year) and $1,972.0 million in FY 2027-28; taxpayers with taxable income under $510,834 pay less on average (about $176) and those above pay more.

measures.title: Keep and Spend Money for Education and Other Purposes
measures.ballot_label: Shall state investment in K-12 public education increase two percent each year for the next ten years, with investments used to increase teacher pay, improve teacher retention, lower class sizes, and increase access to career and technical courses, without raising taxes but instead funded by raising the annual limit on state fiscal year spending ...
plain: Raises the TABOR spending limit by the amount the state spends on K-12 education, so the state keeps money that would otherwise be refunded.
State K-12 funding would grow 2% a year for ten years, for teacher pay, teacher retention, smaller classes, and career and technical courses.
Requires a public, independent annual audit of how the money is spent; no tax rates change.
measures.yes: A yes vote lets the state keep and spend money above the TABOR cap for K-12 education instead of refunding it.
measures.no: A no vote keeps the current TABOR limit and refunds.
measures.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates state spending rises $329.9 million in FY 2026-27 and $521.0 million in FY 2027-28, with TABOR refunds reduced by the same amounts.

measures.title: Increase Penalties for Fentanyl Crimes
measures.ballot_label: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes concerning criminal penalties for fentanyl and certain synthetic opioids, and, in connection therewith, increasing the felony classifications of drug-related crimes for distribution, manufacturing, dispensing, sale, or possession of fentanyl and certain synthetic opioids; creating mandated treatment for certain drug felony violations based on possession amount; ...
plain: Raises the felony level for making, selling, distributing, or possessing fentanyl and certain synthetic opioids.
Requires treatment for some drug felonies, depending on the amount possessed.
Narrows or removes sentencing exceptions for fentanyl crimes and drug-related deaths.
measures.yes: A yes vote increases penalties and adds mandated treatment for fentanyl-related crimes.
measures.no: A no vote keeps current fentanyl penalties and sentencing rules.
measures.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates state spending of $876,488 in FY 2026-27, $8.9 million in FY 2027-28, and $24.8 million in FY 2028-29, mostly for prisons and courts, with mixed effects on local governments.

measures.title: Penalties for Human Trafficking of a Minor
measures.ballot_label: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes modifying existing law concerning human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude, and, in connection therewith, creating new law expanding human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude to include knowingly trading anything of monetary value to buy or sell sexual activity with a minor ...
plain: Makes human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude a class 1 felony, punishable by life in prison without parole or release.
Expands the crime to include knowingly trading anything of value to buy or sell sexual activity with a minor.
Applies to offenses committed on or after January 1, 2027.
measures.yes: A yes vote requires life in prison without parole for trafficking a minor for sexual servitude.
measures.no: A no vote keeps the crime a class 2 felony with the current 8-to-24-year sentence range.
measures.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff expects no state cost until about FY 2041-42, when prison costs rise by roughly $180,000, growing to $360,000 a year, with minimal local impact.

measures.title: Male and Female Participation in School and Collegiate Sports
measures.ballot_label: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes creating new law restricting participation in all K-12 and collegiate school sports based on the participant's sex as determined by certain aspects of their biological reproductive system, and, in connection therewith, requiring a school, institution of higher education, or athletic association ...
plain: Every K-12 and college team or sport must be labeled male, female, or coed, and students may play only on the team matching their sex as defined by biological reproductive system, or on a coed team.
A female may join a male team if no female team exists.
Bars agencies and athletic associations from punishing schools for keeping separate female teams; the education commissioner enforces it for K-12.
measures.yes: A yes vote requires school and college sports teams to be separated by sex as defined in the measure.
measures.no: A no vote keeps current rules on team participation.
measures.fiscal: No state revenue or spending change is estimated; the Department of Education and school districts may see minimal workload and policy-update costs.

measures.title: Prohibit Surgery on Minors in Response to Perception of Sex or Gender
measures.ballot_label: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes modifying existing law by prohibiting surgery on a minor for the purpose of altering the minor's biological sex characteristics, and, in connection therewith, prohibiting any health-care professional or other person from knowingly performing, prescribing, administering, or providing any surgery to a minor ...
plain: Bans health-care professionals and others from performing or providing surgery on anyone under 18 to alter the minor's biological sex characteristics.
Bans using state or federal funds, Medicaid, or insurance coverage to pay for such surgery.
Takes effect January 1, 2027.
measures.yes: A yes vote prohibits sex-altering surgery on minors and public or insurance payment for it.
measures.no: A no vote keeps current law, which does not prohibit these surgeries.
measures.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff expects minimal fiscal impact, with possible small savings in Medicaid and state employee insurance and minimal added workload for regulators and courts.

measures.title: Income Tax Rate Limit
measures.ballot_label: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes capping the state income tax rate at 4.4% of federal taxable income for individuals and corporations?
plain: Makes the current 4.4% income tax rate the maximum rate for individuals and corporations, starting in tax year 2027.
Does not change the rate anyone pays today.
Conflicts with Amendment 87; if both pass, the one with more votes controls where they conflict.
measures.yes: A yes vote caps Colorado's income tax rate at 4.4% in state law.
measures.no: A no vote leaves the legislature and voters free to set the rate above 4.4% in the future.
measures.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff assesses the measure as having no fiscal impact because it keeps the existing 4.4% rate.

measures.title: Direct Sporting Goods Sales Tax Revenue for Conservation
measures.ballot_label: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes creating new law to increase water and land conservation funding without raising taxes, and, in connection therewith, through a voter-approved revenue change, allowing the state to keep and spend a portion of revenue from the state sales tax on sporting goods and equipment ...
plain: Lets the state keep and spend sales tax revenue from sporting goods and equipment instead of refunding it under TABOR.
The money would go to water, land, and forest conservation, wildfire prevention, and outdoor recreation.
Spending could be reduced if needed to protect funding for certain tax credits; no tax rates change.
measures.yes: A yes vote directs sporting-goods sales tax revenue to conservation and wildfire prevention without a TABOR refund.
measures.no: A no vote leaves that revenue subject to current TABOR refund rules.
measures.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates about $175.0 million in FY 2027-28 and $180.2 million in FY 2028-29 redirected to conservation, reducing TABOR refunds by $175.0 million in FY 2027-28, with state spending rising to $54.9 million and then $131.8 million (excluding GOCO).

_uncertain: CO: Amendment 87 and Proposition 136 are competing measures; if both pass, the one with more votes controls conflicting provisions (per Ballotpedia).
